rv.q: The action splinters into little groups, which splits the focus, leads to awkward stop-start pacing and leaches away any build-up of tension or real sense of jeopardy.

But then, like Pete (Owen McDonnell), who falls down the stairs after fighting Diana (Nancy Carroll) with a candlestick and then lies under a sheet for most of the first half, Manor hits us over the head a lot, crashes about, and then gets tired.
Yet, her incidental serrated wit aside, what begins on a note of promising peculiarity dwindles into an editorialising ding-dong between rival emissaries of traditionalist and multicultural Britain.
In fact the second half is basically nonsense, a daft ideological clash that’s too silly to hit home forcefully, but too serious to work as an out-and-out comedy.
There are moments when you can feel it painfully straining for relevance.

But ultimately, Manor is a peculiar disappointment, a damp squib that never ignites: not funny enough to earn its stripes as a black comedy, nor incisive enough to say anything particularly prescient about the UK’s political situation.
A weird, Leftie, apocalyptic state-of-the-nation drama with an Agatha Christie set, it bangs on to little purpose.
The rest of this show, despite a drawling, gumbooted Nancy Carroll as the chatelaine (name of Lady Diana), is dire.
Not surprisingly, Fiona Buffini's production fails to make sense of her sister's madcap misadventure, which is neither dramatically serious nor obviously funny.
But even as a light-hearted Christmas show, this feels little short of a turkey.

Buffini’s breathtakingly inept satire, a state-of-the-nation piece about a collection of one-dimensional characters trapped in a decrepit manor house during an earth-shattering storm, lurches from one improbable scene to another before sinking with all hands.
The National has served-up a magnificent malevolent maelstrom.
It’s a shame that the text is much blunter, giving us starkly oppositional viewpoints instead of trusting us to discover those ideas through the actual people.
Fiona Buffini, directing scenes spread out across this large set, doesn't achieve the intensity of real confrontation.
Its current state, in which it tries to be both, is jarring – and this production could also lower the sheer hamminess by several notches.

After its brilliant set-up, it always feels as if it is straining towards its purpose, with its characters as symbols rather than as real, rooted human beings whose actions will let its points unfold more naturally.

This muddled drama doesn’t know where to pitch itself as it tries to be all things to all people in a multistranded approach that can’t quite bring together its themes of class, history and identity politics.
As a comic satire it is only fitfully funny, and as a state-of-the-nation drama it never gives itself enough room to thoroughly explore the ideas it introduces.
This cluttered script is well outside Buffini’s normal range.
The very fact that I wanted more is evidence that I was enjoying it.
Overall this was a thought provoking, entertaining and subtle play.

There are some interesting moments on the gaslighting of minorities by the far-right, but there’s hardly anything revelatory in Manor’s interrogation of fringe politics – instead it struggles to find something original.

cn.t: Critics find this state-of-the-nation satire muddled and overstuffed, struggling to balance country house mystery, political commentary, and climate themes. Most fault its clumsy execution and one-dimensional characters, though a few praise its ambitious black comedy.
